status: candidate design data; faction identities and balance remain open
designPrinciple: Shared human species, shared physical laws, overlapping mission requirements; distinct industrial, doctrinal, cultural, and historical solutions.
rules: Faction identity must be legible from silhouette, arrangement, and operational behavior before insignia or color is visible.
Style must emerge from doctrine, industrial base, logistics, maintenance, political priorities, and historical lessons; do not reduce a faction to a paint scheme.
All factions can build ships for the same mission class. They differ in how they satisfy its constraints, what they sacrifice, and what they can sustain.
Every signature feature has a physical cost, benefit, maintenance burden, production implication, or tactical consequence.
Common interfaces and captured or exported ships may blur the silhouette; faction identity is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule.
The design profiles below are archetype experiments, not assignments to the thirteen major factions and not real-world nation-to-faction mappings.

styleDimensions.meaning: Hull outline, proportions, massing, and recognizable negative space
Arrangement of command, crew, engineering, propulsion, payload, and protection zones
Armor placement, compartmentation, shielding assumptions, and willingness to expose serviceable components
Duplication, separation, isolation, graceful degradation, and repairability
Engine spacing, mount geometry, plume management, and service access
Manufacturing tolerances, modularity, standardization, finish, and replacement philosophy
Visibility, access, watch stations, maintenance paths, and how human work shapes the vessel
Insignia, surface language, ceremonial features, stencils, and propaganda layered over functional design
Typical field repairs, replaceable panels, reinforcement patterns, and scars from prior doctrine

profiles.label: Mass, separation, and redundancy
profiles.designTendency: Large structural margins, separated critical systems, conservative access routes, substantial compartment boundaries, and visible serviceability.
silhouetteCues: broad shoulders or separated side bodies
failureAndRepairExpression: obvious access covers and isolation boundaries

profiles.label: Dense integration and compactness
profiles.designTendency: Compact envelopes, tightly integrated systems, shared service trunks, and high capability per unit of hull volume.
failureAndRepairExpression: larger repair effort when integrated trunks are damaged

profiles.label: Distributed modules and adaptation
profiles.designTendency: Distinct mission modules, visible attachment structures, replaceable pods, and hulls that can be reconfigured between deployments.
operationalStrengths: rapid mission conversion when modules are available
tradeoffs: logistics burden from many module types
failureAndRepairExpression: empty hardpoints and visibly mixed-generation equipment

profiles.label: Forward concentration and decisive engagement
profiles.designTendency: Command, sensing, and mission systems concentrated toward the expected engagement direction, with strong directional optimization.
tradeoffs: vulnerable blind or rear sectors if neglected
industrialDependencies: doctrine that manages approach and withdrawal
failureAndRepairExpression: urgent aft and flank inspections after maneuvering damage

profiles.label: Dispersed signature and deception
profiles.designTendency: Separated emitters, ambiguous external geometry, distributed decoys, and deliberate control of observable signatures.
tradeoffs: signature discipline can constrain crew convenience
failureAndRepairExpression: obvious loss of deception when damaged elements are not restored

profiles.label: Standardized production and fast service
profiles.designTendency: Repeated hull families, accessible standard parts, clear lifting points, and design choices optimized for fleet availability rather than individual perfection.
failureAndRepairExpression: mixed batches and field modifications visible across older hulls

missionComparisonContract.rule: Compare ships only after matching mission, operating environment, payload, crew, endurance, and technology era.
missionComparisonContract.prohibitedShortcut: Do not assign a universal faction quality score or assume one visual style is always superior.
